title: How To Set Up A Simple, Effective Classroom Management Plan
author: Michael Linsin
summary: This article lays out the mechanics of building a basic classroom management plan from scratch, presenting it as a foundation that lets teachers hold students accountable without yelling, scolding, or lecturing. Linsin recommends four broad, unambiguous rules covering listening and following directions, raising hands, keeping hands and feet to oneself, and respecting classmates and the teacher, arguing their lack of ambiguity discourages arguing and finger-pointing. He then specifies a three-tier consequence system, warning, time-out, and a letter home, describing how time-out should be physically set up as a symbolic rather than punitive separation. Practical details include posting rules and consequences on poster board, resetting the consequence cycle each day, and keeping the letter-home form factual and free of editorializing. The piece closes by reminding readers that a written plan has no power on its own; consistent, faithful follow-through is what makes it effective.
points: Adopt four broad, unambiguous rules covering listening, hand-raising, personal space, and respect, since simplicity discourages arguing and finger-pointing.
Back rules with a three-step consequence ladder, warning, time-out, letter home, so accountability doesn't disrupt classroom flow.
Set up time-out as a symbolic, not punitive, separation, with a desk that's simply set apart rather than isolated or shaming.
Reset consequences daily, so lessons are learned and grudges are dropped by the next morning, giving every student a fresh start.
Keep the letter-home form factual and free of editorializing or anger, since 'how you use it is what gives the plan its power,' not the document itself.
quotes: The purpose of a classroom management plan is to hold students accountable for misbehavior—without having to yell, scold, or lecture.

These rules work because they make sense to students, they’re fully enforceable, and they cover all the bases. Also, because of their refreshing lack of ambiguity, they discourage arguing, complaining, and finger pointing.
It is the symbolic separation from the rest of the class, and the feelings it evokes, that makes time-out effective. It’s not a separation of humiliation or gloomy punishment.

Create a simple form letter to send home to parents when students reach the third and final consequence. Keep it short and to the point. Refrain from giving your opinion or adding an angry note at the bottom.

The consequences are in play throughout one single day. When the students arrive for school the next day, lessons have been learned, no grudges are held, and everyone starts fresh—with another chance to succeed, to grow, to be better than the day before.
This is key, because there is no magic in the plan itself. It’s just a set of guidelines scrawled on a piece of paper. How you use it is what gives the plan its power.
